title.title: Introduction to Smart Contracts
title.subtitle: Why a business would use one, what it really changes, and what it cannot do

why.heading: Why a smart contract at all?
why.subtitle: Business already has three ways to make a deal stick. Run one deal through each, then through code on a shared chain.
why.hint: Click each option to run the same deal through it

deal.label: One deal
deal.text: A Lisbon importer pays a Shenzhen supplier €50,000 once the goods arrive.

options.title: A lawyer
options.role: Writes the deal on paper; courts enforce it afterwards
options.trust: The legal system to put things right afterwards
options.time: Months or years if it ends up in court
options.cheat: Either side can break the deal first; you sue later.
options.weak: Slow, expensive, and enforcement stops at the border.

options.title: An escrow agent
options.role: Holds the €50,000 until both sides deliver
options.time: Days of waiting, plus a fee on every deal
options.cheat: Buyer and supplier are held to it, but the agent has the money.
options.weak: The agent can make mistakes, stall or go bust.

options.title: A company database
options.role: One firm keeps the record and runs the rules
options.cheat: The owner can edit the record; everyone else takes their word.
options.weak: Fine inside one firm. Rivals will not accept a record that one of them controls.

options.title: A smart contract
options.role: Code holds the €50,000 and releases it when delivery is confirmed
options.trust: Code everyone can read, run by a network no one party controls
options.time: Seconds to minutes, for a network fee
options.cheat: No one can bend the rule once it is live.
options.weak: It does exactly what is written, bugs included, and it needs a reliable data feed to know the goods arrived.

recap.heading: The 20-second version
recap.leadB: . Here is the same idea in one picture, then the bridge into the business of it.
recap.definitionLabel: A smart contract in three pieces
recap.vendingBody: Nobody approves it and nobody can talk it round. That is Nick Szabo's 1994 picture of a smart contract.
recap.imgAlt: A vending machine as a smart contract metaphor: right coins in, snack out; wrong coins, money back; no clerk.

cards.title: One shared computer
cards.desc: Thousands of machines run the same code and must agree.

cards.title: Fixed, public rules
cards.desc: Anyone can read the code; no one can quietly change it.

cards.title: Every action has a fee
cards.desc: You pay the network for each step.

cards.title: A person moves first
cards.desc: It only acts when someone sends a signed instruction.

recap.footerText: the business of it. Not how the code works, but when it is worth using.

history.heading: Thirty years in six moments
history.subtitle: Click along the line: from an idea with nothing to run it on to $100B+ in live contracts.

events.title: Szabo coins "smart contract"
events.desc: Nick Szabo describes promises enforced by a mechanism instead of a person. Nothing yet exists that can run one.
events.lesson: A good idea is not a business until the infrastructure exists.

events.title: Ethereum goes live
events.desc: The first chain built to run any agreement as code. The idea finally has a computer.
events.lesson: Once anyone can deploy a rule, experiments multiply fast.

events.title: The DAO loses $60M
events.desc: A bug lets an attacker drain a fund that has no manager to stop it.
events.lesson: Code enforces mistakes as faithfully as intentions.

events.title: Tokens get a common format
events.desc: Shared standards for money-like and one-of-a-kind tokens let any wallet or marketplace handle any asset.
events.lesson: Common standards, not clever code, are what create a market.

events.title: DeFi Summer
events.desc: Contracts start calling other contracts: lending and trading with no bank or broker in the middle.
events.lesson: Contracts become building blocks, and so do their risks.

events.title: High stakes, audited
events.desc: $100B+ sits in contracts across many chains; $6B+ has been lost to exploits since 2016.
events.lesson: Treat a contract as financial infrastructure: audit it before money goes in.

exercise.heading: Contract or not?
exercise.subtitle: Six real situations. Is a smart contract a good fit, or would a company database or a human decision do the job better?
exercise.resultSc: Good fit for a smart contract

scenarios.title: Flight-delay insurance
scenarios.desc: An insurer promises: if your flight lands more than two hours late, you are paid automatically, with no claim form.
scenarios.reason: A simple rule triggered by a public fact. The payout is locked in, so the customer does not have to trust the insurer to honour it. It still needs a reliable feed of arrival times.

scenarios.title: A streaming subscription
scenarios.desc: You pay one company a monthly fee to watch its video library.
scenarios.reason: One company owns the content, the accounts and the billing, and you already trust it with your card. Nobody else needs to check the rule, so an ordinary database is cheaper.

scenarios.title: Fault in a car accident
scenarios.desc: Two drivers disagree about who caused a crash and how much the damage is worth.
scenarios.reason: This needs someone to weigh evidence and decide what is fair. Code can only run a rule that was fixed in advance; it cannot judge.

scenarios.title: All-or-nothing crowdfunding
scenarios.desc: Hundreds of strangers pledge money to a project. If the target is not reached by the deadline, everyone is refunded.
scenarios.reason: Strangers, pooled money and a rule that is pure arithmetic: target met by the deadline, or not. Code can hold the funds, so no platform has to be trusted with them.

scenarios.title: Splitting a song's income
scenarios.desc: Three co-writers agree that every payment the song earns is divided 50 / 30 / 20 between them.
scenarios.reason: A fixed split between several parties who would otherwise rely on one manager's accounting. Code divides each payment as it arrives, for all to see.

scenarios.title: A company's payroll
scenarios.desc: One employer pays its own staff every month and corrects mistakes when they happen.
scenarios.reason: One employer, its own records, and errors that must be reversible. A public rule that is hard to change would expose salaries and make corrections difficult.

quiz.question: Three rival freight companies and their insurer want one shared rule: pay compensation automatically when a shipment arrives late. What is the strongest reason to run that rule as a smart contract instead of in one company's database?
options: It is cheaper and faster to run than a database.
No single company has to be trusted to run the rule, and none of them can quietly change it.
The code automatically counts as a legally binding contract between them.
It can use judgement to treat unusual cases fairly.
quiz.explanation: Rivals will not accept a rule that sits in one competitor's database, because its owner could change it. A smart contract gives them one rule that no single party controls. The other answers are the hype: a database is cheaper and faster, code is not a legal contract by itself, and a smart contract has no judgement, so it runs exactly what was written.

quiz2.question: A supermarket chain wants to move its loyalty points "onto the blockchain". Points are earned and spent only in its own stores. What is the best advice?
options: Go ahead: a smart contract would make the points cheaper to run.
Do not: a smart contract cannot keep track of balances.
Do not: one company issues and controls the points, so its own database does the same job for less.
Go ahead: customers would then own points the chain could never cancel.
quiz2.explanation: A smart contract pays off when several parties need a rule that none of them controls. Here one trusted company issues, prices and redeems the points, so there is no one else to convince and a database is cheaper. The other answers fail on the facts: every on-chain step costs a network fee, contracts track balances perfectly well (that is what tokens are), and points spent only in the chain's own stores are worth whatever the chain decides to honour.

quiz3.question: In 2016 an attacker drained about $60M from The DAO, an investment fund run entirely by a smart contract. What should a business take from that episode?
options: A contract runs exactly what was written, flaws included, so it must be audited before money goes in.
The Ethereum network itself was broken into, so public chains are unsafe.
Smart contracts are too simple to hold large sums.
Contract code should be kept secret so that attackers cannot read it.
quiz3.explanation: The network worked as designed. The flaw was in the contract's own code, and the code did exactly what it said, with no manager able to step in and stop it. That is why contracts holding real money are audited before launch. Hiding the code is not the fix: public code is what lets everyone check the rule they are relying on.

takeaways.title: Section 01 — Key Takeaways
items: A smart contract is self-running code on a shared chain: vending-machine logic, no clerk
Its real competitors are a lawyer, an escrow agent and a company database
Not a legal contract, not smart, not free, not unstoppable
The value: removing a middleman, locking a rule for everyone, settling fast across borders
If one trusted institution already runs the process well, a database will usually win
Thirty years of lessons, from The DAO onwards: code enforces bugs as faithfully as features

hype.heading: Hype or genuine value?
hype.subtitle: Seven things people say about smart contracts. Send each one to the side where it belongs.
hype.binHypeEmpty: Oversold claims land here, with what is actually true.
hype.binValueEmpty: Claims that hold up land here, with the reason.
hype.guessWrong: You put this on the other side

claims.claim: The code is the contract. No lawyers needed.
claims.why: Code moves assets; whether a court recognises it is a separate question. Real deployments pair it with a normal legal agreement.

claims.claim: Rivals can share one rule without trusting each other, or a middleman.
claims.why: No party has to be the trusted one in the middle, or be paid for it.

claims.claim: It is smart: it copes with whatever comes up.
claims.why: It does exactly what is written, with no judgement. A bug runs as faithfully as a feature.

claims.claim: No middleman, so it is basically free.
claims.why: Every step costs a network fee, and storing data on-chain is very expensive.

claims.claim: Once it is live, nobody can quietly bend the rule.
claims.why: True for everyone, operator included, as long as no admin key was left in.

claims.claim: Nobody can ever switch it off.
claims.why: Its website, data feeds and admin keys are ordinary points of control. Tornado Cash's website went dark in 2022 while the contract kept running.

claims.claim: It settles across borders in minutes, around the clock.
claims.why: No banking hours and no correspondent banks, and it leaves a public audit trail.

hype.footer: Ask of every use case: does it need one of the three on the right? If not, a database will usually win.

keyPoints.s1-why: A smart contract earns its place only when one shared, un-bendable rule beats trusting a lawyer, an agent or a database owner.
keyPoints.s1-recap: A smart contract is self-running code on a shared chain: vending-machine logic, no clerk.
keyPoints.s1-hype: Not legal, not smart, not free, not unstoppable; the value is removing a middleman, locking a rule and settling fast.
keyPoints.s1-exercise: A smart contract fits when parties who do not trust each other share a rule that code can check. With one trusted owner, or a judgement call, it adds cost, not trust.
keyPoints.s1-history: Every expensive lesson in thirty years came from code doing exactly what it was told.
